Tedae namah ngawn tah, heah he hnin rhih koep rhing dae. Te daengah ni Khohni loh nang taengah tueng ham a ngaih boeih te a tueng pueng eh,” a ti. Te phoeiah tah kan n'caeh tak coeng.   
\s1 Pilnam Loh Ezra a Paan
Hnin rhih a poeng hil khopuei la ka mael pawt te pilnam loh boeih a yaak vaengah tah, boeih tingtun uh. A yit lamloh a len hil khaw ka taengah la ha loh tih ol a thui uh.
“Kaimih loh nang metlam kan tloelh, nang soah a tloh la balae ka saii uh, balae kaimih nan toeng tih he hmuen la na ngol?
Tonghma boeih khuiah nang bueng loh kaimih nan caeh tak, tawnhnu kah misur bom bang mai la, khohmuen hmuen kah hmaithoi bang mai la, hlipuei lamkah aka daem sangpho bangla.
Kaimih nan hno va atah Zion a ung vaengah ka tlum uh palueng vetih kaimih ham then bet mai mako.
Ka duek uh lakah aka then he kaimih a om moenih,” a ti uh. Te vaengah amih te a ol a len la rhap uh.
Te dongah amih te, “Israel aw namning sak, Jakob imkhui ah kothae sak boeh.
Khohni loh nang m'poek tih Tlungluen loh na thingthuelnah te a hnilh moenih.

Kai khaw, nangmih te kan hnoo pawt tih, nangmih taeng lamloh ka vi uh moenih. Zion a pongnah kong ah thangthui ham neh, mamih kah rhokso a tlayaenah kawng dongah rhennah bih ham ni he hmuen la ka caeh.
Nangmih te na im la boeih mael uh laeh, tahae khohnin phoei lamkah tah tangmih taengla ka lo bitni,” ka ti nah.
Te dongah amih taengkah ka thui bangla pilnam khaw khopuei la cet uh.
Tedae kaimah ngawn tah puencawn kah olpaek bangla khohong ah hnin rhih ka ngol pueng. Khohong kah rhaipai te dawk ka caak tih amah te vaeng tue kah baelhing te ka buh la om.
A hnin rhih a poeng kah hlaem ah tah mang ka man bal.
Ka mang ah tuipuei lamkah khohli ha pawk tih tuiphu a huek khungdae te ka hm uh.

Ka sawt vaengah tuipuei tuilung lamkah aka thoeng te khohli loh hlang muei bangla a saii. Hlang te vaan khomai neh a ding te khaw ka hm uh. A maelhmai sawt hamla a mael vaengah a hamitangnah boeih te tah thuen uh.
A ka lamkah ol a huel vaengah aka ya boeih te hmai loh khoirhat a kaeng vaengkah bangla boeih tlae.
Koep ka sawt vaengah pilnam hlangping te toeklekna pawt la ka hm uh. Amih te vaan khohli loh a coi tun tih tupuei lamkah aka thoeng hlang te vathoh thil hamla pai uh.
Ka sawt bal vaengah mol puei pakhat phuel uh tih a soah a kah te ka hm uh.
Mol aka phuel uh te melamkah nim tila a hmuen a hma te ka sawt dae ka hmu pawh.
Te phoeiah ka sawt hatah amah taengkah aka tingtun boeih loh amah taengah caem la thoo uh. Mueirhih neh khuk bae ngawn dae yong ham huem uh pawh.
Hlangping kah a huk a cuuk tea hmuh vaengah khaw a kut thueng pawt tih, caai neh caemtloeknah caemboh khaw muk pawh.
Tedae a ka lamloh hmai tuiva bangla, a hmuilai lamloh hmai hu bangla, a lai dong lamloh hmaidi konglong bangla a hlah te ka hm uh.

He hmai tuiva neh hmaihu khaw, hlipuei khohli khaw tun hol uh tih a hmuh vaengah tah hlangping khaw yong hamla dae amih te boeih ung. Te dongah hlangping taelekna pawt te bang hma tih laivai hmai phu neh hmaikhu bo bueng la dawk cul. Ka sawt vaengah ka ngaihmang coeng.
Te phoeiah tlang lamkah hlang pakhat ha suntlak thuk te ka hm uh. Amah loh a tloe hlangping taengah rhoepnah la khue uh.

Te phoeiah anih taengla hlang hlang muep ha pawk, hlangvang omngaih tih hlangvang a kothae uh, hlangvang tah a khih uh tih, hlangvang loh a tloe te nawnnah la a khuen uh. .  
\s1 Mathui kah Thuingaihnah  
 Ka haenghang vaengah mueirhih a lenkoek om tih Khohni taengla ka thangthui
Te vaengah, “A tongnah lamloh na sal taengah khobae rhambae khaw nan tueng coeng. Ka thangthuinah na yaak ham ni a tingtawk la kai nan cawh.
Mang kah a thuingaihnah khaw kan nan tueng bal coeng he.
Ka lungbuei ah tah ka boelh het coeng. Anunae te a hlun rhoek ham aih te.
Amih te kothae la hlun mahpawt nim?
Amih tah a hnukkhueng khohnin hamla a khueh hno te a yakming uh dae amih ah doe uh pawh.
Anunae a hlun rhoek aih te, poeknah khaw om coeng. Amih te mueihrhih a len khaw, ngaihhlih a tloh khaw, na mang kah a tueng bangla a hmuh uh ni.

He rhoek hno khuila la a kun ham khaw then mai coeng. Tlohthae loh tlak thil sitoe cakhaw lunglai lamloh khomong bangla cing vetih, khohnin hnukkhueng ah aka thoeng ham te hmu pawt nim?” ka ti.  
 Amah loh kai n'doo tih,
“Mangthui kah thuingaihnah kan thui vetih nang kan thuinuet hno te nang ham kan thuicaih bitni.
Na thui bangla aka suvaih rhoek kah a kawng te khaw, aka suvaih pawt kah a kawng khaw a thuingaihnah tah he pawn ni.
Te vaengah tue ah puenthae aka khuen loh puenthae khuila ka tla rhoek khaw a tungaep ni. Amih tloengkhoelh taengah bibi neh tangnah aka khhueh rhoek te tah.
Te dongah a hlun rhoek tah aka duek rhoek lakah a yoethen ngai tila yakiming .
Mangthui kah a thuingaihnah te he pawn ni. Tuipuei lamkah aka luei hlang na hmuh lah ko.
Anih tah Khohni Pathen loh dieklai tue te yet a khoem hlang yueng pawn ni. A suentae hlahkung la amah om vetih a hlun rhoek te khaw a hoihaeng ni.
Na hmuh bangla a ka lamloh khohli, hmai neh hlipuei thoeng lahko.
Caai khaw coemtloenah pumcum khaw pom pawt dae, anih ta hamla hlangping loh a cuk thil vaengah amih te a thup, he a thuingaihnah coeng ni.
Khohnin ha pai vetih Khohni loh diklai dongkah rhoek te a loeih sak pawn ni.
Diklai khosa rhoek taengah lungbuei cikcoknah pai ni.
Khat neh khaw, khopuei neh khopuei, hmuen khat neh hmuen khaw, pilnam neh pilnam, ram neh ram caemtloeknah om ni.
Hekah hno loh hmuen a loh hlanah ni lamhma la nang miknoek kan tueng. Ka Capa khaw ha thoeng pawn ni. Anih te tuipuei lamkah aka thoeng hlang la na hmuh coeng.
Namtom boeih loh a ol a yaak vaengah, namtom boeih loh amah khohmuen khaw, khat neh khat taengkah rhalthohnah te khaw a toeng ni.
Toekleknah mueh hlangping te huek tingtun vetih na hmuh bangla, cae ham neh anih ta ham te a ngaih uh ni.
Zion te ha pai vetih pilnam boeih taengah a phoenah te a khueh ni. Rhuengphong tih a sak coeng, na hmuh vangbangla kut a om mueh la tlang khundun lah ko.
Ka capa amah loh namtom kah a lailaknah dongah a coi te a toel ham te hlipuei minoek la tueng coeng.

A boethae bangla a maelhmai ah a tlung vetih phaepnah neh amih a kolh te miknoeknah la hmai om coeng. Olkhueng kah a thuingaihnah dongah a tlungmu pawt dongah amih a thup ham te miknoeknah la hmai a tueng sak coeng.
A taengah ngaimong la hlangping a coi bal te khaw na hmuh coeng.

Amih te manghai Hoshae tue vaengah a kho lamloh vangsawn la a khuen koca pako rhoek ni. Amih te Assyria manghai Shalmaneser loh saldong la a khueh. Amih te tuiva a kat puei tih khohmuen tloe la a khuen.
Tedae amamih hamla mangtaengnah a khueh, namtom hlangping te caeh tak tih khohla ngai la caeh hamla. Te hmuen ah tah hlang hing loh kho a sak noek moenih.
Tedaengah ni amah khohmuen ah a tuem uh pawt a oltloek te a tuem uh eh.
Amih te Perath tuiva kah solong a caeknah longah cet uh.
Te khohnin lamkah tah Khohni loh amih ham miknoek a tueng sak. Bawt a kat uh hil tuiva kah tuilong te a kueng pah.
Khohmuen pingpang te a caeh long khaw sen tih, a yincaehnah te kumkhat neh tintan lo. Tekah khohmuen tah Arzareth la a khue.
Te phoeiah a tue hnukkhueng hil kho a sak uh. Amih te khaw koep halo tom coeng.
Khohni loh tuiva kah tuilong te koep a kueng bal ni. Tedaengah ni tuiva te a kat uh thai eh. Te dongah hlangpin loh ngaimong la hueng a tingtun uh te na hm uh.
Tedae na pilnam a hlun rhoek te tah ka khorhi cim ah phoe uh tih daem uh ni.
Te dongah huek aka tingtun namtom te a thup vaengah aka sueng rhoek tah amah loh a tungaep ni.
Amih te kopoekrhai muep a tueng ni.
“Tloengkhoelh Boeipa aw kai hamla han thuicaih la saw, balae tih tupuei tuilung lamkah hlang a luei te ka hmuh,” ka ti.

Kai taengah, “Tuipuei kah a dungnah he a phuelh neh aka ming he khat khaw a om pawt bangla, tahae khohnin kah mueh tah ka Capa khaw a khuikah aka om rhoek khaw aka hmu thai he diklai ah khat khaw om pawh.
Mang na hmuh kah a thuingaihnah tah he ni.
Na longpuei te na hnoo tih na pum te kai ham la na khueh dongah ka olkueng khaw na khe coeng.
Na hingnah khaw cueihnah dongah na tlungmu tih yakmingnah te na nu la na khue.

Te dongah hekah hno he nang kan tueng coeng. Na thapang ngawn tah Khohni taengah a khueh coeng. Hnin thum a poeng phoeiah tah ol a tloe kan thui pueng ni. Nang taengah dumlai aka rhih neh, kopoekrhai te ka thuicaih pueng ni,” a ti.
Te phoeiah ka thoo tih lohma li ah ka pongpa, a hnin, hnin ah Khohni loh kopoekrhai a saii dongah thangpomnah neh koehnah a lenkoek ka paek.
Amah loh a tue neh amah khoning a poeng hil aka thoeng hno boeih te a uktaem. Te phoeiah hnin thum pahoi ka om pueng.
\s1 Boeipa loh Ezra a Tueihnah
A hnin thum dongkah thingnu hmuiah ka ngol, ka hmaidan kah tangpuem khui lamloh ol ha thoeng tih, “Ezra, Ezra!,” a ti.
Te dongah ka doo tih, “Boeipa ka om he,” ka ti nah tih ka kho dongah ka pai.
Te vaengah amah loh kai te, “Kai he tangpuem dongah ka phoe tih, ka pilnam loh Egypt kah hloong dongah a om vaengah Moses t eka voek.
Anih te ka tueih tih ka pilnam te Egypt lamloh ka mawt. Anih te Sinai tlang la ka khuen tih kamah taengah khoyin a yet ka om puei.
Anih te kopoekrhai ol muep ka thui pah tih a tue kah olhuep khaw ka tueng. A tue a bawtnah khaw anih taengah ka phong pah. Te vaengah anih ka uen tih,
He ol he tah langya la hoe lamtah he bal tah a huep la khoem,” ka ti nah.
Na taengah miknoek kan tueng soah na thinko hong lah. Mang te khaw na man coeng tih a thuingainah khaw na yaak coeng.
Hlanghing lakli lamloh nang n'loh saeh lamtah a tue a bawtnah hil, ka capa nen khaw, namah bangla aka om rhoek nen khaw khosa uh.
Camoe kah kum te a hma atah a patong tue ni a tong coeng.
Diklai tue he a boelnah hlainit la a paekboe tih, a boel pako tah khum coeng.
A boel parha te khaw rhakthuem coeng tih, a boel parha dongkah rhakthuem neh boel nit ni a om coeng.
Te dongah na imkhui te khaw khueh laeh, na pilnam te toel laeh. Amih khuikah tlayae rhoek te hloep laeh, aka cueih rhoek khaw thuituen laeh. Aka hmawn pawh hingnah te thui laeh.
Pumsa poeknah dul lamtah hlanghing kah hnorhih te namah lamloh voei laeh. Na coengnah kah vawtthoeknah te khaw hal laeh.
Na aka naan ngaih na poeknah khaw khat ben tla rhoe lamtah tahae tue lamloh a loe la nong laeh.
He lamkah tah na hmuk lakah aka nah ngaih yoethaenah tah hmuen a loh pawn ni.
Thahnoeng ham tah lunglai he phat patong hang coeng tih khosa boeih soah khaw boethae he ping hang coeng.

Oltak tah a hla la cet coeng tih laithae tah a yoei la ha pawk coeng. Te nih na mangthui dongah a loe la atha ha lo te na hm uh.   
\s1 Cabu Cim Koep A Daek
Te vaengah ka doo tih, “Na mikhmuh ah ka thui mai eh Boeipa.

Kai nan uen bangla ka cet vetih pilnam aka hing pueng rhoek te ka toel ni. Tedae tahae lamkah a cun rhoek tah uh long a toel eh? Lunglai he hmaisuep la yalh tih khosa rhoek khaw hmaivang mueh la om uh.
Na olkhueng khaw a hoeh uh coeng tih, nang loh na saii tangtae neh na saii ham koi hno te aka ming khat khaw om voel pawh.

Na taengah kolonah ka dang atah ka khuiah cim mueihla han tueih lah. A tong cuek lamloh lunglai dongah aka thoeng te khaw, na olkhueng dongkah a daek olka te khaw ka daek pawn eh. Te daengah ni pilnam loh a caehlong a hmuh thai vetih a hnukkhueng ah hing aka ngaih rhoek long a vai uh eh,” ka ti nah.
Amah loh kai n'doo tih, “Cet lamtah pilnam te coi laeh, amih te thui pah lamtah khohni sawmli khuiah nang n'tlap uh boel saeh.
Namah hamla cadaek cabael muep tawn lamtah, na taengah Sarea, Dabria, Selemia, Ethanus neh Asiel te khuen. Amih panga loh a daek ham te hlinsai laeh.
He la koep na lo vaengah yakimingnah hmaithoi te na thinko ah kan tok bitni. Ca boeih na daek hil tekah kan thih mahpawh.

Boeih na daek vaengah hno rhakthuem te langya la khueh lamtah, rhakthuem tah yinhnuk ah hlangcueih taengah khuen uh. Cadaek ham te thangvuen khonoek he vaengah tong laeh,” a ti.   
\s1 Pilnam ham Ol Hnukkhueng
Kai n'uen bangla ka cet tih pilnam te tun ka coi.
Te vaengah ah, “Israel aw olka he ya uh lah.
Lamhma ah a pa rhoek Egypt ah hlanglak bangla kho a sak uh tih te lamloh koep ana loeih uh.
Hingnah olkhueng a dang uh dae tuem uh paw, amih phoeiah khaw tekah te na poe uh bal.
Zion khohmuen ah na koerhang la nangmih te khohmuen m'paek bal. Tedae nangmih neh na pa rhoek long khaw boethae a saii uh tih Khohnin loh nangmih n'uen te khaw a longpuei bangla na tuem uh pawh.
Amah tah aka dueng laitloekung la a om dongah a tue a rhoek vaengah tah nangmih m'paek te khaw koep a lat.
Te dognah nangmih khaw, na pilnam khaw khorhi khuiah a hlahloei la na om uh coeng.
Tedae na lungbuei te na taem tih na thinko te na hlinsai atah nangmih te a hing la n'khoem vetih na dueknah hnukah khaw haidamnah na dang uh ni.
Dueknah hnukah tah laitloeknah ha pai ni. Mamih koep n'hing uh vaengah aka duengkah ming tah phoe ni. Khoboe lailak rhoek tah a bil pawn ni.

Tedae kai taengah la khat khaw ha lo uh boel lamtah hnin sawmli khuiah khat long khaw kai n'tlap uh boeh,” ka ti nah.   
\s1 Cacim Koep A Daek
Kai n'uen bangla hlang panga ka khueh tih lohma la ka thoeih uh tih pahoi ka rhaeh uh.
A vuen ah ol pakhat loh kai n'khue tih, “Ezra na ka ang lamtah ok ham kam paek te o lah,” a ti.
Te dongah ka ka ka ang hatah kai te boengloeng a bae la m'paek. Te te tui bangla muep om dae a pangcik tah hmai bangla om.
Te te ka loh tih ka ok. Ka ok vaengah ka thinko te yakmingnah loh a bueih. Ka rhangsuk dongah cueihnah bae. Ka mueihla hamla poeknah phoe.
Te dongah ka ka ka ang te ka khuep voel pawh.

Hlang panga rhoek te khaw Khohni loh yakmingnah a paek. Te dongah a ciim la aka om te daek ham hoi uh. Me bang catham a hnonah khaw ming uh pawh. Hnin sawmli ngol uh tih khothaih ah a daek uh, khoyin daengla buh a caak uh.
Kamah ngawn tah khothaih ah ka thui tih khoyin ah khaw kam ka khuem pawh.
Te dongah cabu somko pali he khohnin sawmli ah ka daek uh.
Hnin sawmli a cup phoeaiah tah Khohni loh m'voek tih, “Na daek lamhma cau pakul pali te langya la khueh lamtah, amih te a tiing neh a tiing pawt khaw tae sak.
Tedae a hnuk la parhih na daek rhoek te tah khoem lamtah na pilnam khuikah aka cueih taengah pae.
A khuiah yakmingnah sokca, cueihnah tuisih, mingnah tuiva om lah ko,” a ti.
\s1 Halang Taengah Tholh Thungnah
Tonghma ol te ka pilnam hna ah thui pah, tete na ka dongah kang khueh bitni, Boeipa long ni a thui.
Amih a tingtawk neh oltak la aka om rhoek tah cahawn dongah daek sak.
Nang aka taeng rhoek te khaw rhih boeh, aka tangmueh rhoek loh nangmih n'tloelh dongah ngaihmang sak uh boeh.
Aka tangnah mueh tah a tangnah pawt bangla duek uh ni.
Boeipa loh a thui he ngaithuen, lunglai soah puenthae, cunghang neh khokha, dueknah neh pocinah ka khuen ni.
Tholhiknah he kho takuem ah cet coeng tih, rhih om la a saii uh khaw a khuetnah a pha coeng.
Te dongah Boeipa loh a thui coeng.

Khoboe lailak neh a bawt mueh la a sainah kawng dongah kam ka khuem pawt vetih, halang kah omihnah khaw ka ueh mahpawh. Ommongsitoe neh hlang dueng kah a thii he kai taengah pang coeng. Hlang dueng kah hinglu khaw phat pang coeng.
Amih te phu ka loh ni, Boeipa loh a ti lah ko. Amih lamkah ommongsitoe thii neh boeih ka loh ni.
Ka pilnam te ngawnnah kungah boiva bangla a mawt uh coeng ke. Egypt khohmuen ah khosak hamla ka hlah voel mahpawh.
Tedae amih te tlungluen kut neh, ban ka lam neh ka loh vetih, Egypt te lucik neh lamhma kah bangla a khohmuen te boeih ka phae ni.
Egypt neh a khoengim rhoek te nguekcoi laeh saeh, Boeipa loh a soah toelnah lucik neh cawhnah te a lung pah pawn ni.
Lotawn khaw lairhi duela nguekcoi saeh, a cang ti te a poe ham khaw ut coeng tih a thingkung te mawn neh, rhael neh, khonal tuihli loh a phae coeng.
Anunae, lunglai neh a khuikah khosa rhoek boeih ham aih te.
Cunghan neh citcaih tah amih taengla yoei coeng, namtom loh namtom tloek hamla a thoh thil ni, a kut dongkah cunghang nen te.
Pilnam taengah hinghongnah om aka tlung loh aka lung a rhoeng thil ni, a tlungtluen loh te a manghai neh khoboei boeilu rhoek hinyah mah pawh.
Hlang loh khopuei khuila cet ngaih mai cakhaw a saii ham noeng van mahpawh.
A koevoeinah dongah khopuei rhoek khaw kilkul uh vetih imlo a phae uh vaengah pilnam long khaw a rhih ni.
Pilnam loh a imben soah lungma ti mah pawt vetih amih te cunghang neh a cawk ni. A hno te khaw a poelyoe pah ni. Te khaw a bungpong uh tih longlonah muep a om coeng dongah ni.

Diklai manghai boeih te ka taengla mael ham tun ka khueng coeng he ne. Pathen loh a ti coeng lah ko, khomik a thoengnah lamkah khaw, tuithim lamkah khaw, khocuk neh Lebanon lamkah khaw, amih taengah ka paek te ha mael saeh lamtah n'thuung laeh saeh.
Tahae khohnin hil ka tuek rhoek taengah a saii uh bangla amih taengah ka saii vetih a rhang dongah ka thuung ni. Te dongah Boeipa loh he ni a thui.
Ka bantang kut loh hlang tholh te hlun pawt vetih, ka cunghang loh diklai ah ommongsitoe thii aka long sak taeng lamloh paa mahpawh.
A kosi dong lamloh hmai a caeh hlue atah, diklai neh hlangtholh kah khoengim te boeih a hlawp tih, divawt bang lamni a ung mai.
Anunae, tholh tih ka olpaek aka tuem pawt rhoek aih te, Boeipa loh a thui coeng lah ko.
Amih te ka hnaih mahpawh. Khoe uh laeh hoeih, nangmih hnukpoh ca rhoek aw, ka rhokso he poeih uh boeh.
Amah taengah aka tholh khaw Pathen loh a ming dongah ni amih te dueknah neh aka ngawn kut dongla a voeih.

Diklai pum ah yoethaenah ngawn tah pai tangtae coeng dae te khuiah ah ni na hing uh. Pathen loh nangmih n'hlawt mahpawh, amah taengah na tholh uh dongah.   
\s1 Caemtloek Hamla Hmuh saknah
Khothoeng lamkah aka phoe te mikhmuh ah thuen tangkik. Arabia kah tuihnam namtom tah leng neh muep ha thoeng.
Te khohnin atha hlah uh tih diklai hman ah phit uh ni. Te dongah aka ya boeih tah rhihnah neh thuen uh ni.

Carmonian khaw kosi neh kawk tih duup lamloh khohong okrhul bangla khong uh pawn ni. Thadueng len neh ha pawk vetih coemtloenah ah rhong a pai ni. A pumcunah a no loh Assyria khohmuen kah khoyo te boeih a thoe pah ni.
Tedae tuihnam rhoek tah a hnun a poek vetih a thadueng koep om ni, a thaomnah te a len la a cului vetih amih te a hloem ni.
Te vaengah amih te taekyaek uh ni, a thadueng paa vetih a mael neh rhaelrham uh ni.

Te vaengah Assyria khohmuen lamkah rhal tah a rhongngol vetih amih a tloek ni, amih te pakhat la a phae ni. A rhal rhoek soah rhihnah neh thuennah pai vetih a manghai rhoek soah konoi uh ni.   
\s1 Babylon Soah Laitloeknah
Khothoeng lamkah, tlangpuei lamkah neh tuithim lamkha khomai thoeng coeng ke. A suisak khaw a toehnah a puehkan la om tih, kosi neh hlipuei muep bae.
Khat neh khaw boeng uh thae vetih tih diklai dongah thintoinah muep bae ni. Amih kah thintoinah rhangneh cunghang lamkah thii te marhang kah a bungpuei a muelh hil,
hlang kah a pumpu neh kalauk kah a uen hil li ni.
Diklai dongah rhihnah neh thuennah muep om ni. Tete aka hmuh rhoek tah kosi loh a let sak vetih thuennah loh a tuuk ni.
Te phoeiah tah hlipuei khomai tah tuithim lamloh, tlangpuei lamloh, a tloe te khotlak lamloh yolh uh ni.

Tedae khothoeng lamkah kholi long tah kosi neh aka thoeng khomai te a yawn vetih bang cing ni. Pocinah la aka om thintoinah te khaw khothoeng khohli loh a phae vetih khotlak tuithim la phaeng a vai ni.
Khomai len neh aka tlung, kosi thintoi aka hah te ha thoeng vetih diklai pum neh amah khosa te boeih phae ni. A thintoi rhihom te pomdoep hmuen sang boeih ah a hawk ni.
Hmai neh, rhael neh, cunghang aka ding neh, tuilii tui mai neh, lohma neh sokko boeih khaw tekah tui ni muep a bae eh.
Khopuei neh pangbueng khaw, tlang neh mol khaw, duup kah thing khaw, rhamtlim baelhing khaw, a vueithaih khaw a thup ni.
A kaepvai te khaw a paan uh vetih, a thintoi neh a thinsanah boeih te a hawk thil uh ni. Te vaengah laipi neh laivai te vaan la luei vetih a kaepvai ah nguekcoi uh ni.

Aka sueng rhoek loh a phae rhoek te a khut ni.   
\s1 Asia soah Laitloeknah
Asia nang khaw Babylon kah rhuepomnah neh a thangpomnah aka bawn van ni.

Anunae, nang aih te, pocinah khomap coeng. Anih bangla na sa uh khangrhoep bal. Na kolo taengah tah na tanu khaw pumyoi la na det tih, na hlang ngaih neh, na hmatoeng kah aka cukhalh rhoek taengah na thangpom.
A khoboe neh a poeknah boeih dongah thiinah ham aka om te na awt. Te dongah Pathen loh,
‘Nang soah yoethaenah kan tueih vetih, nuhmai, khodaeng, khokha, cunghang, duektahaw ka tueih vetih tih, na im khaw a imrhong la pai ni, dueknah neh cungkunah hang khuen ni.
Nang soah kholing kan tueih vaengah na thadueng thangpomnah khaw rhaipai bangla rhae ni.
Huta a boh tih hmasoe ah a rhawp bangla na kha ni. Te dongah na hlangtlung na lungnah te khaw na doe thai mahpawh,’ a ti.
Nang te thalaeng kan saii ni, Boeipa loh a ti coeng lahko.
Ka pillnam hlang coelh phat na ngawn te khaw, na thangpom te, na kut na paeng te khaw, na rhui vaengah a dueknah na thui uh te mah ana toeng boeh.
Na hmai te ana hluk ngawn.
Na pumyoih kah thaphu te na baeng ah kap lah ko. Te dongah namah dantatnah na dang pawn ni.
Boeipa loh a thui lah ko. Ka pilnam hlang coelh na saii bangla Pathen loh nang taengah han saii van ni. Na thunkha kut ah n'tloeng pawn ni.
Na ca rhoek te bungpong ah duek vetih cunghang dongah na kaeh uh ni. Na khopuei rhoek te a khoe vetih khohoeng kah na pilnam boeih khaw, na khohmuen khaw cunghang dongah cungku uh ni.
Tlang neh hmuensang kah aka om rhoek khaw bungpong neh lamlum uh ni. Buh a pong neh amah saa neh a caak uh vetih tui a halh ah amah thii te a ook uh ni.
Te boeih soah kothet khueh uh laeh, na pawk uh vaengah pumsa ah citcai neh na patang uh ni.
A caehpah doela a thiinah khopuei rhoek te a phop uh vetih na khohmuen rhakthuem a phae uh ni. Na thangpomnah khoyo khaw a koengloeng uh ni, Babylon khopong lamkah a mael uh vaengah.
Hmuitoel bangla nangmih te n'ngael uh vetih nangmih taengah hmai la ha poeh uh ni.
Na khopuei khaw, na khohmuen khaw, na molmae khaw a hlawp uh ni. Na duup neh thingkung thingthaih khaw hmai neh a hlup uh ni.
Na ca rhoek te tamna la a khueh vetih na khuehtawn te a poelyoe uh ni, na diklung diklai kah thangpomnah khaw a baeh uh ni.
\s1 Hmailong kah Kokhahnah
Anunae Babylon neh Asia nang aih te! Anunae Egypt neh Syrian nang aih te!
Tlamhnin vaep lamtah maae mul mah bai laeh.
Nang soah cunghang han tueih coeng dongah u lae a hnuk la aka mael eh?
Na soah hmai han tueih coeng tih, unim aka thih lah ve?
Nang soah citcai han tueih coeng tih u long nim a vai lah ve?
Duup kah sathueng bungpong he aka vai khat khaw om nim? Hmai khaw vai hlup aka rhong keh aka thih thai om nim?
Lithen hlangtlung loh a kah palaa ke aka mael sak khat khaw om nim?
Boeipa Pathen loh citcai a tueih coeng tih u long te a haek thai eh?
A thinsa lamloh hmai thoeng vetih, u long a thih thai eh?
Amah te rhaek lah khophaa aka cu te u long a rhih pawt pai eh? Amah te khohum la a hum te u lae a thuen pawt pai eh?
Boeipa loh a toeh pawn ni, a mikhmuh ah ulae rhep aka yoka pawt pai eh?
Diklai neh a khoengim khaw tuen. Tuitun li khaw a laedil lamloh samboek coeng. Tuiphu neh a khukah nga rhoek khaw Boeipa neh a sarhi thangpomnah hmaiah limlum saeh.

A bantang kut loh a lii a tang kalak te a phuk coeng, A palaa loh pat a kah vetih diklai a bawtnah duek pakhat khaw a hmaai mueh la a kah ni. A palaa tah haa tih a kutnoek te a pit pawt dongah diklai a bawtnah hil rhenten a kah.
Citcai te a tueih phai coeng dongah diklai hman a pha hil ha mael mahpawh.
Hmai a tok coeng dongah diklai khoengim a tlum duela thih voel mahpawh.
Tlungluen lithen loh palaa aka bangla mael mah pawh. Te dongah diklai dongah citcai a tueih te mael mahpawh.

Ya-oe kai aih, ya-oe kai aih he, te khohnin vaengah u long nim kai n'hlawt lah ve?   
\s1 Hnukkhueng Khohnin kah Puenthae

Kothaenah a tongnah cuek ah, rhaengsaenah khaw muep om ni. Khokha a tong vaengah muep lamlum uh ni. Rhalpuei a tong vaengah sarhi khaw boeih let ni. Citcai a tong vaengah boeih thuen uh ni. Cicai a pai tanglang vaengah balae a saii uh eh?
Khokha neh lucik, longlonah neh norhuengnah tah hlanghing aka toel ham hmaitak bangla a tueih coeng.
He boeih a om lalah a boethae lamloh mael uh pawt tih toelnah rhuihet khaw lungbuei ah khueh uh pawh.
Diklai ah buh maeh bahoeng yoei tih pilnam loh mongnah ngaikhuek la om ni tila mang ana tuk ngawn saeh. Diklai ah citicai te sunghang la, khokha la, ngaihmang khobing la ha phuet bitni.
Khokhang dongah diklai khosa rhoek muep lamlum uh vetih, khokha loh a caknoi rhoek te cunghang dongah duek uh ni.
Aka duek rhoek te aek bangla a voeih uh vetih amih aka suem te khat khaw om mahpawh. Diklai he khopong la a hno uh vetih khopuei khaw boeih a koengloeng uh ni.
Khohmuen aka tawn neh aka tuh ham pakhat khaw paih mahpawh.
Misur te hmuen cakhaw u long a sui eh? Hmuen takuem ah a dingrhak la boeih om ni.
Hlang loh a tloe kah hlang te hmuh ham te, hlang ol yaak ham te a hue uh ni.
Khopuei pum neh lohma ah khaw hlang rha bueng, thingko neh lungko ah aka thuk rhoek khaw panit bueng ni a paih eh.
Olive a yoep uh vaengah khaw olive thing pathum pali ni a paih eh.
Misur dum kah a bit uh vaengah ngaithuen la aka so rhoek long pataenga a bom a yol ni a paih pa eh.
Te khohnin ah tah cunghang neh amih im aka khe rhoek loh pathum pali ni a paih eh.
Diklai te khopong la a hno vetih khohmuen te a yoe pah ni. Longpuei lamhlawn ah hling a buk vetih boiva khaw yuel mahpawh.
Tongpa a om pawt dongah oila khaw nguek ni. Tongpa a om pawt dongah manu rhoek khaw nguek ni. Bomkung a tal dongah tanu rhoek nguekcoi uh ni.

Yulokung rhoek te caem loh a ngawn pah vetih a va rhoek khaw khokha ah lamlum uh ni.   
\s1 Pathen Pilnam kah Rhueng Phongnah
Ol he hnatun laem lamtah yakming laeh, nang tah Boeipa kah sal ni.
He tah Boeipa kah ol ni. Te te doe lamtah Boeipa loh a thui te hnalval boeh.
Citcai he yoei coeng tih uelh voel mahpawh.
Huta bungvawn bangla, hla ko vaengah tah a ca-om tue loh yoei vaengah, lamhma la khonoek panit pathum vaenagh a bung bahoeng tlo tingtuel coeng. Te dongah camoe a om ham khaw a koe voel moenih.
Te dongah diklai dongla citcai aka loh uelh mahpawh, lunglai ngawn tah kopang vetih a tloh la hmuen takuem boeih a tuuk ni.
Ka pilnam aw, ka ol hnatun lah. Diklai dongah kholong bangla citcai lakli ah caemtloek la hlah uh laeh.
Hno yoi khaw aka rhaelrham bangla, hno lai khaw aka hlong bangla om uh laeh.
Bitat aka saii khaw a hoeikhangnah aka dang pawt bangla, im sa khaw a khui ah aka om pawt bangla,
cang aka tu khaw aka at pawt bangla, misur aka hloe long khaw a thaih aka yoep pawt bangla,
yulo vasa khaw camoe aka cun pawt bangla, yulo vasa mueh khaw nuhmai bangla, om saeh.
Thakthae rhoek khaw a poeyoek la thakthae coeng.
Kholong loh a thaih a yoep pa vetih a koe a poelyoe pah ni. A im a palet pa vetih a ca rhoek te a sol pah ni. Tamna neh khokha vaengah a ca a khue uh ni.
Tangka aka tlap khaw dawk a hmu vetih phaeng a khuen pah ni. Muep aka khueh a khopuei, a him, koerhang a hlang thoeihcam saeh.
A tholhnah bangla amih taengah ka thinsanah muep ka khuen pah ni a ti Boeipa long ni a thui.
Hinyah kap neh bihaam nu loh pumyoi a tuei bangla,

hlang dueng loh boethae a tuei. A hmuh vaengah a nai bahoeng kap mai cakhaw. Diklai dongkah tholhnah boeih aka khe loh a hmai, hmai ah rhep a dang vaengah u long anih a rhun eh?   
\s1 Pathen Kah Cueihnah
Anih neh anih kah khoboe bangla om boeh.
Diklai lamloh boethae a khoe ham te a tue bahoeng toi ca tih duengnah loh mamih n'uk pawn ni.
Hlang tholh loh ka tholh pawh ti boel saeh, “Pathen neh amah thangpomnah hmaiah ka tholh pawh,” aka ti boeih kah a lu soah Pathen loh hmai alh a poep pa ni.
Pilnam kah a saii boeih te Boeipa loh rhep a ming. Amih kah mangtuk neh a poeknah khaw, a thinko khaw a ming.
“Diklai om saeh,” a ti tih om tangloeng. “Vaan khaw om saeh,” a ti tih om tangloeng.
A ol loh aisi khaw amah hmuen ah tluep a om sak tih, aisi kah a mi khaw boeih a ming.
Tangrhom dung neh a thakvoh khaw a khe, tuitunli neh a hmuenma khaw boeih a nueh.
Tui laklung ah tuitun khaw a khueh tih, a ol rhangneh diklai khaw tui soah poe.
Impuei bangla vaan khaw a yaal tih, a soah khaw tui khaw a khoem.
Khosoek ah tuisih a khueh tih tlang som ah tuibuem a khueh. Te dongah hmuen sang lamloh tuiva a long sak tih diklai ah tui a paek.
Hlang hing te a hlombol tih a pum laklung ah a thinko a khueh pah. Hlang te hil, hingnah neh yakmingnah,
tlungthang Pathen mueihla te rhip a paek. Amah loh a cungkuem te a saii tih a huephael hmuen kah a huephael te khaw a khe.
Nang khaw, na mangtuk neh na thinko kah na poeknah khaw a ming.
Anunae aka tholh tih a tholhnah aka hlipdah rhoek aih te. Boeipa loh a khoboe boeih te rhep a cawh pah vetih nangmih boeih khaw langya n'tai pawn ni.
Na tholhnah te hlang tloe taengah a phoe vaengah yah na poh bitni. Te khohnin ah na boethae te nang tholh aka phoe la pai ni.
Balae na saii van eh? Boeipa neh a thangpomnah hmai ah na tholhnah te metlam na phan eh?

Pathen he laitloekkung la om ngawn saeh. Amah te rhih lamtah na thohlnah lamloh paa laeh. Na boethae khaw hnilh ltam a khuila koep kun voel boeh. Boeipa long m'mawt saeh lamtah longlonah cungkuem lamloh na loeih bitni.   
\s1 Pathen Pilnam Hnaemtaeknah
Kosi hmairhong loh nangmih kah hlangping muep a hoeh coeng. Nangmih lamkah a ngen tah a doek vetih mueirhol maeh te caak ham a tanolh ni.
Amih te tah na rhoi atah nangmih te n'lawn ni, n'nueihnah ni, n'hlak ni.
Khopuei taengkah hmuen takuem ah Boeipa aka rhih rhoek ham hnaemtaek, kuthlahnah om ni.
Hlang tloek rhooek tah hlang lueng rhoek bangla om uh ni. Boeipa aka rhih rhoek te lungma ti muehla a poelyoe vetih a thup uh ni.
Amih kah koerhang te a poelyoe uh vetih a im neh imkhui lamloh amih te a vai uh ni.

Te vaengah ka tuek hlang rhoek a noemcai vetih a rhilh hmai loh sui a noem cai bangla a rhilh te phoe ni.   
\s1 Pathen kah Hlawtnah Olkhueh
Ka hlang tuek rhoek aw hnatun uh lah, Boeipa loh a thui lahko. Longlonah hnin tah kut dongah om coeng, a khui lamloh nangmih kan hlawt pawn ni.
Nang tah ka olpaek neh olrhi te na khoem coeng. Na tholhnah loh nang n'nan boel saeh lamtah, na boethae loh nang m'vuei boel saeh.
Anunae a tholhnah loh a ven tih a boethae loh a thing rhoek aih ke. Amih te lota loh a thing lohma bangla om tih a namtlak khaw hling malh sai. Tedongah aka pah thai khat khaw om pawh.
Te tah khobing coeng tih hmai long ni a hlawp mai coeng.

headers.cabu: he cueinah ol neh a boelrhai la om tih kotue rhamtang ah rhaengpuei loh a tae mai coini. Judah hlang khatkhat loh Greek ol la a tael cabu la om. A taelnah khohni uh loh ming pawt dae
headers.yacut: pali tluk vaengah a tael. Olpuei koek la kohlopnah boeih te Pathen tangnah, poeknah neh khingmong tumbaem a ngoe kawng a thui. .
headers.ip: Cadaekkung long he Greek rhoek kah poeknah neh a tong dae Pathen ah tangnah kawng neh pitpom sak pawh. He cabu loh a lungui la a thui koek tah Moses Olkhueng dongah uepom la om he ni cueinah a kung la a thui. Cimphan la poek tih Pathen tangnah neh bibinah long pilnam khaw uehnah, kuemsuemnah, rhalthennah, hlangtloe taengah langya la omnah ham a rhoeng sak. Cadaekung loh thuinuetnah muep a paek. A pacuek ah tah Baibal dongkah patuel mingthang rhoek thuinuetnah la thui. Te lamlong tah Eleazar neh Makkabi Cabu pabae a boel 3-6 dongkah boeinaphung pathum kawng a tui. A cimphan la poeknah long tah pilnam he patangnah, hnaemtaeknah khui ah khaw ueh nah a paek thai tila a thuicaih. Tahae tue kah tangca pilnam ham khaw a cimphan la poek tih Pathen tangnah he hinglu ham dungyan hingnah ti hmuh thai.
headers.io1: Poekcimnah neh Pathen tangnah loh a thae a ta (5.1—18.24)

verses.text: \s1 Cabu Thuicaihnah
He kawng dongah poeknah kawng ni muep thuicaih ham ka cai. Poeknah cimphan la a om atah kohlopnah khaw boeih a ta. Te dongah kamah long tah poeknah kawng dongah na hnatung ham he ka ngaih.
Hekah a kawng he mingnah aka tlap boeih ham olpuei la om tih a sang koek khoboe then koehnah neh a thap. Te dongah a thuem la khingmongnah kawng he a thui.
Te daengah ni kuemsuem nah aka dah kung carhut neh hoehhamnah boeih te taemrhai thai eh.
Kohlopnah he thailainah la om tih tiktamnah a kanghalh khaw cimphan la tueng ngawn. Aming la thui koinih thinsanah, rhihnah, tlohyaknah long he thinomnah khaw a nong tak.

A ngen loh, “Khingmongnah loh kohlopnah a uk atah, balae tih hnilhmanah neh hnalvalnah tah a uk pawh?” a ti uh. Amih kah veet tih a oelhnah khaw nueih thaboep!\f + \fr 1.5 \ft Or \fq Kai kah oelhnah he nueih thaboep la a saii uh!\f*
Khingmongnah loh amah kohlopnah te a uk ngawn moenih. Tedae kohlopnah loh tiktamnah, rhalthennah, kuemsuemnah khaw a phae. Khingmongnah khaw te rhoek aka phae ham pawt tih aka hoihaeng ham ni a om.
Khingmongnah loh kohlopnah a uktaem kawng te muep kan tueng thai.
Tedae hingcimnah dongah rhalthen la aka duek Eleazar boeinaphung parhih neh a manu dongah aka tueng he then koek.
Khingmongnah loh kohlopnah a tumbaemnah te a tueng dongah ni dueknah aka pai sak patangnah khaw a hnaep thai.

Tahae tue vaengah khaw amih kah omih koeh ham he kai hlinsai. Amih mai tah a manu khaw rhuepomnah neh thennah kong ah duek. Amih kah a then saii dongah hinyahnah neh amih te yoethen hlang la ka khue pai.

Pilnam boeih he a phaep dae amihkah rhalthennah dongah a kopoekrhai uh. Hlangmuen rhoek kongah nih a ram ah amih a cungku uh. Tedae uehnah rhangneh hlangmuen khaw a ta dongah amih rhangneh a ram khaw a cim sak.

He kawng he a tawibawt la ka thui mai eh, he tlam ni ka khosing van rhoe. A ning ka hol tih ka rhan bangla a kawng te ka thui phoei ah cueihnah cungkuem Pathen ka thangpom eh.   
\s1 The Supremacy of Reason
A longim la ka khe vaengah lungpoeknah he kothlopnah lakah khuet.
Lungpoeknah he blae, kohlopnah he balae ti khaw oltloek lah sih. Kohlopnah he a hui muep om dae tekah rhoek boeih te lungpoeknah lo a ta.
Now reason is the mind that with sound logic prefers the life of wisdom.
Wisdom, next, is the knowledge of divine and human matters and the causes of these.
This, in turn, is education in the law, by which we learn divine matters reverently and human affairs to our advantage.
Now the kinds of wisdom are rational judgment, justice, courage, and self-control.
Rational judgment is supreme over all of these, since by means of it reason rules over the emotions.
The two most comprehensive types\f + \fr 1.20 \ft Or \fq sources \f* of the emotions are pleasure and pain; and each of these is by nature concerned with both body and soul.
The emotions of both pleasure and pain have many consequences.
Thus desire precedes pleasure and delight follows it.
Fear precedes pain and sorrow comes after.
Anger, as a person will see by reflecting on this experience, is an emotion embracing pleasure and pain.
In pleasure there exists even a malevolent tendency, which is the most complex of all the emotions.
In the soul it is boastfulness, covetousness, thirst for honor, rivalry, and malice;
in the body, indiscriminate eating, gluttony, and solitary gormandizing.
Just as pleasure and pain are two plants growing from the body and the soul, so there are many offshoots of these plants,\f + \fr 1.28 \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq these emotions\f*
each of which the master cultivator, reason, weeds and prunes and ties up and waters and thoroughly irrigates, and so tames the jungle of habits and emotions.

For reason is the guide of the virtues, but over the emotions it is sovereign.  
 Observe now, first of all, that rational judgment is sovereign over the emotions by virtue of the restraining power of self-control.
Self-control, then, is dominance over the desires.
Some desires are mental, others are physical, and reason obviously rules over both.
Otherwise, how is it that when we are attracted to forbidden foods we abstain from the pleasure to be had from them? Is it not because reason is able to rule over appetites? I for one think so.
Therefore when we crave seafood and fowl and animals and all sorts of foods that are forbidden to us by the law, we abstain because of domination by reason.
For the emotions of the appetites are restrained, checked by the temperate mind, and all the impulses of the body are bridled by reason.
And why is it amazing that the desires of the mind for the enjoyment of beauty are rendered powerless?
It is for this reason, certainly, that the temperate Joseph is praised, because by mental effort\f + \fr 2.2  \ft Other ancient authorities add \fq in reasoning\f* he overcame sexual desire.
For when he was young and in his prime for intercourse, by his reason he nullified the frenzy\f + \fr 2.3  \ft Or \fq gadfly \f* of the passions.
Not only is reason proved to rule over the frenzied urge of sexual desire, but also over every desire.\f + \fr 2.4  \ft Or \fq all covetousness\f*
Thus the law says, “You shall not covet your neighbor's wife or anything that is your neighbor's.”

In fact, since the law has told us not to covet, I could prove to you all the more that reason is able to control desires.  
 Just so it is with the emotions that hinder one from justice.
Otherwise how could it be that someone who is habitually a solitary gormandizer, a glutton, or even a drunkard can learn a better way, unless reason is clearly lord of the emotions?

Thus, as soon as one adopts a way of life in accordance with the law, even though a lover of money, one is forced to act contrary to natural ways and to lend without interest to the needy and to cancel the debt when the seventh year arrives.

If one is greedy, one is ruled by the law through reason so that one neither gleans the harvest nor gathers the last grapes from the vineyard.  
 In all other matters we can recognize that reason rules the emotions.
For the law prevails even over affection for parents, so that virtue is not abandoned for their sakes.
It is superior to love for one's wife, so that one rebukes her when she breaks the law.
It takes precedence over love for children, so that one punishes them for misdeeds.
It is sovereign over the relationship of friends, so that one rebukes friends when they act wickedly.

Do not consider it paradoxical when reason, through the law, can prevail even over enmity. The fruit trees of the enemy are not cut down, but one preserves the property of enemies from marauders and helps raise up what has fallen.\f + \fr 2.14  \ft Or \fq the beasts that have fallen\f*
It is evident that reason rules even\f + \fr 2.15  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq through \f* the more violent emotions: lust for power, vainglory, boasting, arrogance, and malice.
For the temperate mind repels all these malicious emotions, just as it repels anger—for it is sovereign over even this.
When Moses was angry with Dathan and Abiram, he did nothing against them in anger, but controlled his anger by reason.
For, as I have said, the temperate mind is able to get the better of the emotions, to correct some, and to render others powerless.
Why else did Jacob, our most wise father, censure the households of Simeon and Levi for their irrational slaughter of the entire tribe of the Shechemites, saying, “Cursed be their anger”?
For if reason could not control anger, he would not have spoken thus.
Now when God fashioned human beings, he planted in them emotions and inclinations,
but at the same time he enthroned the mind among the senses as a sacred governor over them all.
To the mind he gave the law; and one who lives subject to this will rule a kingdom that is temperate, just, good, and courageous.
How is it then, one might say, that if reason is master of the emotions, it does not control forgetfulness and ignorance?
But this argument is entirely ridiculous; for it is evident that reason rules not over its own emotions, but over those of the body.
No one of us\f + \fr 3.2  \ft Gk \fq you \f* can eradicate that kind of desire, but reason can provide a way for us not to be enslaved by desire.
No one of us can eradicate anger from the mind, but reason can help to deal with anger.
No one of us can eradicate malice, but reason can fight at our side so that we are not overcome by malice.

For reason does not uproot the emotions but is their antagonist.   
\s1 King David's Thirst
Now this can be explained more clearly by the story of King David's thirst.
David had been attacking the Philistines all day long, and together with the soldiers of his nation had killed many of them.

Then when evening fell, he\f + \fr 3.8  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq he hurried and\f* came, sweating and quite exhausted, to the royal tent, around which the whole army of our ancestors had encamped.
Now all the rest were at supper,
but the king was extremely thirsty, and though springs were plentiful there, he could not satisfy his thirst from them.
But a certain irrational desire for the water in the enemy's territory tormented and inflamed him, undid and consumed him.

When his guards complained bitterly because of the king's craving, two staunch young soldiers, respecting\f + \fr 3.12  \ft Or \fq embarrassed because of\f* the king's desire, armed themselves fully, and taking a pitcher climbed over the enemy's ramparts.
Eluding the sentinels at the gates, they went searching throughout the enemy camp
and found the spring, and from it boldly brought the king a drink.
But David,\f + \fr 3.15  \ft Gk \fq he \f* though he was burning with thirst, considered it an altogether fearful danger to his soul to drink what was regarded as equivalent to blood.
Therefore, opposing reason to desire, he poured out the drink as an offering to God.
For the temperate mind can conquer the drives of the emotions and quench the flames of frenzied desires;

it can overthrow bodily agonies even when they are extreme, and by nobility of reason spurn all domination by the emotions.   
\s1 An Attempt on the Temple Treasury
The present occasion now invites us to a narrative demonstration of temperate reason.

At a time when our ancestors were enjoying profound peace because of their observance of the law and were prospering, so that even Seleucus Nicanor, king of Asia, had both appropriated money to them for the temple service and recognized their commonwealth—
just at that time certain persons attempted a revolution against the public harmony and caused many and various disasters.

Now there was a certain Simon, a political opponent of the noble and good man, Onias, who then held the high priesthood for life. When despite all manner of slander he was unable to injure Onias in the eyes of the nation, he fled the country with the purpose of betraying it.
So he came to Apollonius, governor of Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia, and said,

“I have come here because I am loyal to the king's government, to report that in the Jerusalem treasuries there are deposited tens of thousands in private funds, which are not the property of the temple but belong to King Seleucus.”
When Apollonius learned the details of these things, he praised Simon for his service to the king and went up to Seleucus to inform him of the rich treasure.
On receiving authority to deal with this matter, he proceeded quickly to our country accompanied by the accursed Simon and a very strong military force.
He said that he had come with the king's authority to seize the private funds in the treasury.

The people indignantly protested his words, considering it outrageous that those who had committed deposits to the sacred treasury should be deprived of them, and did all that they could to prevent it.
But, uttering threats, Apollonius went on to the temple.
While the priests together with women and children were imploring God in the temple to shield the holy place that was being treated so contemptuously,

and while Apollonius was going up with his armed forces to seize the money, angels on horseback with lightning flashing from their weapons appeared from heaven, instilling in them great fear and trembling.

Then Apollonius fell down half dead in the temple area that was open to all, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and with tears begged the Hebrews to pray for him and propitiate the wrath of the heavenly army.
For he said that he had committed a sin deserving of death, and that if he were spared he would praise the blessedness of the holy place before all people.

Moved by these words, the high priest Onias, although otherwise he had scruples about doing so, prayed for him so that King Seleucus would not suppose that Apollonius had been overcome by human treachery and not by divine justice.

So Apollonius,\f + \fr 4.14  \ft Gk \fq he \f* having been saved beyond all expectations, went away to report to the king what had happened to him.   
\s1 Antiochus' Persecution of the Jews
When King Seleucus died, his son Antiochus Epiphanes succeeded to the throne, an arrogant and terrible man,
who removed Onias from the priesthood and appointed Onias's\f + \fr 4.16  \ft Gk \fq his \f* brother Jason as high priest.
Jason \f + \fr 4.17  \ft Gk \fq He \f* agreed that if the office were conferred on him he would pay the king three thousand six hundred sixty talents annually.
So the king appointed him high priest and ruler of the nation.
Jason \f + \fr 4.19  \ft Gk \fq He \f* changed the nation's way of life and altered its form of government in complete violation of the law,
so that not only was a gymnasium constructed at the very citadel\f + \fr 4.20  \ft Or \fq high place\f* of our native land, but also the temple service was abolished.
The divine justice was angered by these acts and caused Antiochus himself to make war on them.
For when he was warring against Ptolemy in Egypt, he heard that a rumor of his death had spread and that the people of Jerusalem had rejoiced greatly. He speedily marched against them,
and after he had plundered them he issued a decree that if any of them were found observing the ancestral law they should die.
When, by means of his decrees, he had not been able in any way to put an end to the people's observance of the law, but saw that all his threats and punishments were being disregarded
—even to the extent that women, because they had circumcised their sons, were thrown headlong from heights along with their infants, though they had known beforehand that they would suffer this—
when, I say, his decrees were despised by the people, he himself tried through torture to compel everyone in the nation to eat defiling foods and to renounce Judaism.
The tyrant Antiochus, sitting in state with his counselors on a certain high place, and with his armed soldiers standing around him,
ordered the guards to seize each and every Hebrew and to compel them to eat pork and food sacrificed to idols.
If any were not willing to eat defiling food, they were to be broken on the wheel and killed.

When many persons had been rounded up, one man, Eleazar by name, leader of the flock, was brought\f + \fr 5.4  \ft Or \fq was the first of the flock to be brought\f* before the king. He was a man of priestly family, learned in the law, advanced in age, and known to many in the tyrant's court because of his philosophy.\f + \fr 5.4  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq his advanced age\f*
When Antiochus saw him he said,
“Before I begin to torture you, old man, I would advise you to save yourself by eating pork,
for I respect your age and your gray hairs. Although you have had them for so long a time, it does not seem to me that you are a philosopher when you observe the religion of the Jews.
When nature has granted it to us, why should you abhor eating the very excellent meat of this animal?
It is senseless not to enjoy delicious things that are not shameful, and wrong to spurn the gifts of nature.
It seems to me that you will do something even more senseless if, by holding a vain opinion concerning the truth, you continue to despise me to your own hurt.
Will you not awaken from your foolish philosophy, dispel your futile reasonings, adopt a mind appropriate to your years, philosophize according to the truth of what is beneficial,
and have compassion on your old age by honoring my humane advice?
For consider this: if there is some power watching over this religion of yours, it will excuse you from any transgression that arises out of compulsion.”
When the tyrant urged him in this fashion to eat meat unlawfully, Eleazar asked to have a word.
When he had received permission to speak, he began to address the people as follows:
“We, O Antiochus, who have been persuaded to govern our lives by the divine law, think that there is no compulsion more powerful than our obedience to the law.
Therefore we consider that we should not transgress it in any respect.
Even if, as you suppose, our law were not truly divine and we had wrongly held it to be divine, not even so would it be right for us to invalidate our reputation for piety.
Therefore do not suppose that it would be a petty sin if we were to eat defiling food;
to transgress the law in matters either small or great is of equal seriousness,
for in either case the law is equally despised.
You scoff at our philosophy as though living by it were irrational,
but it teaches us self-control, so that we master all pleasures and desires, and it also trains us in courage, so that we endure any suffering willingly;

it instructs us in justice, so that in all our dealings we act impartially,\f + \fr 5.24  \ft Or \fq so that we hold in balance all our habitual inclinations\f* and it teaches us piety, so that with proper reverence we worship the only living God.

“Therefore we do not eat defiling food; for since we believe that the law was established by God, we know that in the nature of things the Creator of the world in giving us the law has shown sympathy toward us.
He has permitted us to eat what will be most suitable for our lives,\f + \fr 5.26  \ft Or \fq souls \f* but he has forbidden us to eat meats that would be contrary to this.
It would be tyrannical for you to compel us not only to transgress the law, but also to eat in such a way that you may deride us for eating defiling foods, which are most hateful to us.
But you shall have no such occasion to laugh at me,
nor will I transgress the sacred oaths of my ancestors concerning the keeping of the law,
not even if you gouge out my eyes and burn my entrails.
I am not so old and cowardly as not to be young in reason on behalf of piety.
Therefore get your torture wheels ready and fan the fire more vehemently!
I do not so pity my old age as to break the ancestral law by my own act.
I will not play false to you, O law that trained me, nor will I renounce you, beloved self-control.
I will not put you to shame, philosophical reason, nor will I reject you, honored priesthood and knowledge of the law.
You, O king,\f + \fr 5.36  \ft Gk lacks \fq O king\f* shall not defile the honorable mouth of my old age, nor my long life lived lawfully.
My ancestors will receive me as pure, as one who does not fear your violence even to death.
You may tyrannize the ungodly, but you shall not dominate my religious principles, either by words or through deeds.”
When Eleazar in this manner had made eloquent response to the exhortations of the tyrant, the guards who were standing by dragged him violently to the instruments of torture.
First they stripped the old man, though he remained adorned with the gracefulness of his piety.
After they had tied his arms on each side they flogged him,
while a herald who faced him cried out, “Obey the king's commands!”
But the courageous and noble man, like a true Eleazar, was unmoved, as though being tortured in a dream;
yet while the old man's eyes were raised to heaven, his flesh was being torn by scourges, his blood flowing, and his sides were being cut to pieces.
Although he fell to the ground because his body could not endure the agonies, he kept his reason upright and unswerving.
One of the cruel guards rushed at him and began to kick him in the side to make him get up again after he fell.
But he bore the pains and scorned the punishment and endured the tortures.
Like a noble athlete the old man, while being beaten, was victorious over his torturers;
in fact, with his face bathed in sweat, and gasping heavily for breath, he amazed even his torturers by his courageous spirit.
At that point, partly out of pity for his old age,
partly out of sympathy from their acquaintance with him, partly out of admiration for his endurance, some of the king's retinue came to him and said,
“Eleazar, why are you so irrationally destroying yourself through these evil things?
We will set before you some cooked meat; save yourself by pretending to eat pork.”
But Eleazar, as though more bitterly tormented by this counsel, cried out:
“Never may we, the children of Abraham,\f + \fr 6.17  \ft Or \fq O children of Abraham\f* think so basely that out of cowardice we feign a role unbecoming to us!
For it would be irrational if having lived in accordance with truth up to old age and having maintained in accordance with law the reputation of such a life, we should now change our course
and ourselves become a pattern of impiety to the young by setting them an example in the eating of defiling food.
It would be shameful if we should survive for a little while and during that time be a laughingstock to all for our cowardice,
and be despised by the tyrant as unmanly by not contending even to death for our divine law.
Therefore, O children of Abraham, die nobly for your religion!
And you, guards of the tyrant, why do you delay?”
When they saw that he was so courageous in the face of the afflictions, and that he had not been changed by their compassion, the guards brought him to the fire.
There they burned him with maliciously contrived instruments, threw him down, and poured stinking liquids into his nostrils.
When he was now burned to his very bones and about to expire, he lifted up his eyes to God and said,
“You know, O God, that though I might have saved myself, I am dying in burning torments for the sake of the law.
Be merciful to your people, and let our punishment suffice for them.
Make my blood their purification, and take my life in exchange for theirs.”
After he said this, the holy man died nobly in his tortures; even in the tortures of death he resisted, by virtue of reason, for the sake of the law.
Admittedly, then, devout reason is sovereign over the emotions.
For if the emotions had prevailed over reason, we would have testified to their domination.
But now that reason has conquered the emotions, we properly attribute to it the power to govern.
It is right for us to acknowledge the dominance of reason when it masters even external agonies. It would be ridiculous to deny it.\f + \fr 6.34  \ft Syr: Meaning of Gk uncertain\f*
I have proved not only that reason has mastered agonies, but also that it masters pleasures and in no respect yields to them.
For like a most skillful pilot, the reason of our father Eleazar steered the ship of religion over the sea of the emotions,
and though buffeted by the stormings of the tyrant and overwhelmed by the mighty waves of tortures,
in no way did he turn the rudder of religion until he sailed into the haven of immortal victory.

No city besieged with many ingenious war machines has ever held out as did that most holy man. Although his sacred life was consumed by tortures and racks, he conquered the besiegers with the shield of his devout reason.
For in setting his mind firm like a jutting cliff, our father Eleazar broke the maddening waves of the emotions.
O priest, worthy of the priesthood, you neither defiled your sacred teeth nor profaned your stomach, which had room only for reverence and purity, by eating defiling foods.
O man in harmony with the law and philosopher of divine life!
Such should be those who are administrators of the law, shielding it with their own blood and noble sweat in sufferings even to death.

You, father, strengthened our loyalty to the law through your glorious endurance, and you did not abandon the holiness that you praised, but by your deeds you made your words of divine\f + \fr 7.9  \ft Other ancient authorities lack \fq divine \f* philosophy credible.
O aged man, more powerful than tortures; O elder, fiercer than fire; O supreme king over the passions, Eleazar!
For just as our father Aaron, armed with the censer, ran through the multitude of the people and conquered the fiery\f + \fr 7.11  \ft Other ancient authorities lack \fq fiery \f* angel,
so the descendant of Aaron, Eleazar, though being consumed by the fire, remained unmoved in his reason.

Most amazing, indeed, though he was an old man, his body no longer tense and firm,\f + \fr 7.13  \ft Gk \fq the tautness of the body already loosed\f* his muscles flabby, his sinews feeble, he became young again
in spirit through reason; and by reason like that of Isaac he rendered the many-headed rack ineffective.
O man of blessed age and of venerable gray hair and of law-abiding life, whom the faithful seal of death has perfected!
If, therefore, because of piety an aged man despised tortures even to death, most certainly devout reason is governor of the emotions.
Some perhaps might say, “Not all have full command of their emotions, because not all have prudent reason.”
But as many as attend to religion with a whole heart, these alone are able to control the passions of the flesh,
since they believe that they, like our patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, do not die to God, but live to God.
No contradiction therefore arises when some persons appear to be dominated by their emotions because of the weakness of their reason.
What person who lives as a philosopher by the whole rule of philosophy, and trusts in God,
and knows that it is blessed to endure any suffering for the sake of virtue, would not be able to overcome the emotions through godliness?
For only the wise and courageous are masters of their emotions.
\s1 Seven Brothers Defy the Tyrant
For this is why even the very young, by following a philosophy in accordance with devout reason, have prevailed over the most painful instruments of torture.

For when the tyrant was conspicuously defeated in his first attempt, being unable to compel an aged man to eat defiling foods, then in violent rage he commanded that others of the Hebrew captives be brought, and that any who ate defiling food would be freed after eating, but if any were to refuse, they would be tortured even more cruelly.
When the tyrant had given these orders, seven brothers—handsome, modest, noble, and accomplished in every way—were brought before him along with their aged mother.
When the tyrant saw them, grouped about their mother as though a chorus, he was pleased with them. And struck by their appearance and nobility, he smiled at them, and summoned them nearer and said,

“Young men, with favorable feelings I admire each and every one of you, and greatly respect the beauty and the number of such brothers. Not only do I advise you not to display the same madness as that of the old man who has just been tortured, but I also exhort you to yield to me and enjoy my friendship.
Just as I am able to punish those who disobey my orders, so I can be a benefactor to those who obey me.
Trust me, then, and you will have positions of authority in my government if you will renounce the ancestral tradition of your national life.
Enjoy your youth by adopting the Greek way of life and by changing your manner of living.
But if by disobedience you rouse my anger, you will compel me to destroy each and every one of you with dreadful punishments through tortures.
Therefore take pity on yourselves. Even I, your enemy, have compassion for your youth and handsome appearance.
Will you not consider this, that if you disobey, nothing remains for you but to die on the rack?”
When he had said these things, he ordered the instruments of torture to be brought forward so as to persuade them out of fear to eat the defiling food.

When the guards had placed before them wheels and joint-dislocators, rack and hooks\f + \fr 8.13  \ft Meaning of Gk uncertain\f* and catapults\f + \fr 8.13  \ft Here and elsewhere in 4 Macc an instrument of torture\f* and caldrons, braziers and thumbscrews and iron claws and wedges and bellows, the tyrant resumed speaking:
“Be afraid, young fellows; whatever justice you revere will be merciful to you when you transgress under compulsion.”

But when they had heard the inducements and saw the dreadful devices, not only were they not afraid, but they also opposed the tyrant with their own philosophy, and by their right reasoning nullified his tyranny.
Let us consider, on the other hand, what arguments might have been used if some of them had been cowardly and unmanly. Would they not have been the following?
“O wretches that we are and so senseless! Since the king has summoned and exhorted us to accept kind treatment if we obey him,
why do we take pleasure in vain resolves and venture upon a disobedience that brings death?
O men and brothers, should we not fear the instruments of torture and consider the threats of torments, and give up this vain opinion and this arrogance that threatens to destroy us?
Let us take pity on our youth and have compassion on our mother's age;
and let us seriously consider that if we disobey we are dead!
Also, divine justice will excuse us for fearing the king when we are under compulsion.
Why do we banish ourselves from this most pleasant life and deprive ourselves of this delightful world?
Let us not struggle against compulsion\f + \fr 8.24  \ft Or \fq fate \f* or take hollow pride in being put to the rack.
Not even the law itself would arbitrarily put us to death for fearing the instruments of torture.
Why does such contentiousness excite us and such a fatal stubbornness please us, when we can live in peace if we obey the king?”
But the youths, though about to be tortured, neither said any of these things nor even seriously considered them.
For they were contemptuous of the emotions and sovereign over agonies,
so that as soon as the tyrant had ceased counseling them to eat defiling food, all with one voice together, as from one mind, said:
“Why do you delay, O tyrant? For we are ready to die rather than transgress our ancestral commandments;
we are obviously putting our forebears to shame unless we should practice ready obedience to the law and to Moses\f + \fr 9.2  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq knowledge \f* our counselor.
Tyrant and counselor of lawlessness, in your hatred for us do not pity us more than we pity ourselves.\f + \fr 9.3  \ft Meaning of Gk uncertain\f*
For we consider this pity of yours, which insures our safety through transgression of the law, to be more grievous than death itself.
You are trying to terrify us by threatening us with death by torture, as though a short time ago you learned nothing from Eleazar.

And if the aged men of the Hebrews because of their religion lived piously\f + \fr 9.6  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq died \f* while enduring torture, it would be even more fitting that we young men should die despising your coercive tortures, which our aged instructor also overcame.
Therefore, tyrant, put us to the test; and if you take our lives because of our religion, do not suppose that you can injure us by torturing us.
For we, through this severe suffering and endurance, shall have the prize of virtue and shall be with God, on whose account we suffer;

but you, because of your bloodthirstiness toward us, will deservedly undergo from the divine justice eternal torment by fire.”   
\s1 The Torture of the First and Second Brothers
When they had said these things, the tyrant was not only indignant, as at those who are disobedient, but also infuriated, as at those who are ungrateful.
Then at his command the guards brought forward the eldest, and having torn off his tunic, they bound his hands and arms with thongs on each side.
When they had worn themselves out beating him with scourges, without accomplishing anything, they placed him upon the wheel.
When the noble youth was stretched out around this, his limbs were dislocated,
and with every member disjointed he denounced the tyrant, saying,

“Most abominable tyrant, enemy of heavenly justice, savage of mind, you are mangling me in this manner, not because I am a murderer, or as one who acts impiously, but because I protect the divine law.”
And when the guards said, “Agree to eat so that you may be released from the tortures,”
he replied, “You abominable lackeys, your wheel is not so powerful as to strangle my reason. Cut my limbs, burn my flesh, and twist my joints;
through all these tortures I will convince you that children of the Hebrews alone are invincible where virtue is concerned.”
While he was saying these things, they spread fire under him, and while fanning the flames\f + \fr 9.19  \ft Meaning of Gk uncertain\f* they tightened the wheel further.
The wheel was completely smeared with blood, and the heap of coals was being quenched by the drippings of gore, and pieces of flesh were falling off the axles of the machine.
Although the ligaments joining his bones were already severed, the courageous youth, worthy of Abraham, did not groan,
but as though transformed by fire into immortality, he nobly endured the rackings.
“Imitate me, brothers,” he said. “Do not leave your post in my struggle\f + \fr 9.23  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq post forever\f* or renounce our courageous family ties.
Fight the sacred and noble battle for religion. Thereby the just Providence of our ancestors may become merciful to our nation and take vengeance on the accursed tyrant.”
When he had said this, the saintly youth broke the thread of life.

While all were marveling at his courageous spirit, the guards brought in the next eldest, and after fitting themselves with iron gauntlets having sharp hooks, they bound him to the torture machine and catapult.

Before torturing him, they inquired if he were willing to eat, and they heard his noble decision.\f + \fr 9.27  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq having heard his noble decision, they tore him to shreds\f*
These leopard-like beasts tore out his sinews with the iron hands, flayed all his flesh up to his chin, and tore away his scalp. But he steadfastly endured this agony and said,
“How sweet is any kind of death for the religion of our ancestors!”

To the tyrant he said, “Do you not think, you most savage tyrant, that you are being tortured more than I, as you see the arrogant design of your tyranny being defeated by our endurance for the sake of religion?
I lighten my pain by the joys that come from virtue,
but you suffer torture by the threats that come from impiety. You will not escape, you most abominable tyrant, the judgments of the divine wrath.”
\s1 The Torture of the Third and Fourth Brothers
When he too had endured a glorious death, the third was led in, and many repeatedly urged him to save himself by tasting the meat.
But he shouted, “Do you not know that the same father begot me as well as those who died, and the same mother bore me, and that I was brought up on the same teachings?

I do not renounce the noble kinship that binds me to my brothers.”\f + \fr 10.3  \ft Other ancient authorities add verse \fv 4 \fv* \fq So if you have any instrument of torture, apply it to my body; for you cannot touch my soul, even if you wish.”\f*
Enraged by the man's boldness, they disjointed his hands and feet with their instruments, dismembering him by prying his limbs from their sockets,
and breaking his fingers and arms and legs and elbows.

Since they were not able in any way to break his spirit,\f + \fr 10.7  \ft Gk \fq to strangle him\f* they abandoned the instruments\f + \fr 10.7  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq they tore off his skin\f* and scalped him with their fingernails in a Scythian fashion.
They immediately brought him to the wheel, and while his vertebrae were being dislocated by this, he saw his own flesh torn all around and drops of blood flowing from his entrails.
“We, most abominable tyrant, are suffering because of our godly training and virtue,
but you, because of your impiety and bloodthirstiness, will undergo unceasing torments.”
When he too had died in a manner worthy of his brothers, they dragged in the fourth, saying,
“As for you, do not give way to the same insanity as your brothers, but obey the king and save yourself.”
But he said to them, “You do not have a fire hot enough to make me play the coward.
No—by the blessed death of my brothers, by the eternal destruction of the tyrant, and by the everlasting life of the pious, I will not renounce our noble family ties.
Contrive tortures, tyrant, so that you may learn from them that I am a brother to those who have just now been tortured.”
When he heard this, the bloodthirsty, murderous, and utterly abominable Antiochus gave orders to cut out his tongue.
But he said, “Even if you remove my organ of speech, God hears also those who are mute.
See, here is my tongue; cut it off, for in spite of this you will not make our reason speechless.
Gladly, for the sake of God, we let our bodily members be mutilated.
God will visit you swiftly, for you are cutting out a tongue that has been melodious with divine hymns.”
\s1 The Torture of the Fifth and Sixth Brothers
When he too died, after being cruelly tortured, the fifth leaped up, saying,
“I will not refuse, tyrant, to be tortured for the sake of virtue.
I have come of my own accord, so that by murdering me you will incur punishment from the heavenly justice for even more crimes.
Hater of virtue, hater of humankind, for what act of ours are you destroying us in this way?
Is it because\f + \fr 11.5  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq Or does it seem evil to you that\f* we revere the Creator of all things and live according to his virtuous law?

But these deeds deserve honors, not tortures.”\f + \fr 11.6  \ft Other authorities add verses 7 and 8, \fv 7 \fv* \fq If you but understood human feelings and had hope of salvation from God— \fv 8 \fv* \fq but, as it is, you are a stranger to God and persecute those who serve him.”\f*
While he was saying these things, the guards bound him and dragged him to the catapult;

they tied him to it on his knees, and fitting iron clamps on them, they twisted his back\f + \fr 11.10  \ft Gk \fq loins \f* around the wedge on the wheel,\f + \fr 11.10  \ft Meaning of Gk uncertain\f* so that he was completely curled back like a scorpion, and all his members were disjointed.
In this condition, gasping for breath and in anguish of body,
he said, “Tyrant, they are splendid favors that you grant us against your will, because through these noble sufferings you give us an opportunity to show our endurance for the law.”
When he too had died, the sixth, a mere boy, was led in. When the tyrant inquired whether he was willing to eat and be released, he said,
“I am younger in age than my brothers, but I am their equal in mind.
Since to this end we were born and bred, we ought likewise to die for the same principles.
So if you intend to torture me for not eating defiling foods, go on torturing!”
When he had said this, they led him to the wheel.
He was carefully stretched tight upon it, his back was broken, and he was roasted\f + \fr 11.18  \ft Other ancient authorities add \fq by fire\f* from underneath.
To his back they applied sharp spits that had been heated in the fire, and pierced his ribs so that his entrails were burned through.
While being tortured he said, “O contest befitting holiness, in which so many of us brothers have been summoned to an arena of sufferings for religion, and in which we have not been defeated!
I also, equipped with nobility, will die with my brothers,
and I myself will bring a great avenger upon you, you inventor of tortures and enemy of those who are truly devout.
We six boys have paralyzed your tyranny.
Since you have not been able to persuade us to change our mind or to force us to eat defiling foods, is not this your downfall?
Your fire is cold to us, and the catapults painless, and your violence powerless.
For it is not the guards of the tyrant but those of the divine law that are set over us; therefore, unconquered, we hold fast to reason.”
\s1 The Torture of the Seventh Brother
When he too, thrown into the caldron, had died a blessed death, the seventh and youngest of all came forward.

Even though the tyrant had been vehemently reproached by the brothers, he felt strong compassion for this child when he saw that he was already in fetters. He summoned him to come nearer and tried to persuade him, saying,
“You see the result of your brothers' stupidity, for they died in torments because of their disobedience.
You too, if you do not obey, will be miserably tortured and die before your time,
but if you yield to persuasion you will be my friend and a leader in the government of the kingdom.”

When he had thus appealed to him, he sent for the boy's mother to show compassion on her who had been bereaved of so many sons and to influence her to persuade the surviving son to obey and save himself.
But when his mother had exhorted him in the Hebrew language, as we shall tell a little later,
he said, “Let me loose, let me speak to the king and to all his friends that are with him.”
Extremely pleased by the boy's declaration, they freed him at once.
Running to the nearest of the braziers,

he said, “You profane tyrant, most impious of all the wicked, since you have received good things and also your kingdom from God, were you not ashamed to murder his servants and torture on the wheel those who practice religion?
Because of this, justice has laid up for you intense and eternal fire and tortures, and these throughout all time\f + \fr 12.12  \ft Gk \fq throughout the whole age\f* will never let you go.

As a man, were you not ashamed, you most savage beast, to cut out the tongues of men who have feelings like yours and are made of the same elements as you, and to maltreat and torture them in this way?
Surely they by dying nobly fulfilled their service to God, but you will wail bitterly for having killed without cause the contestants for virtue.”
Then because he too was about to die, he said,
“I do not desert the excellent example\f + \fr 12.16  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq the witness\f* of my brothers,
and I call on the God of our ancestors to be merciful to our nation;\f + \fr 12.17  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq my race\f*
but on you he will take vengeance both in this present life and when you are dead.”

After he had uttered these imprecations, he flung himself into the braziers and so ended his life.\f + \fr 12.19  \ft Gk \fq and so gave up\ft ; other ancient authorities read \fq gave up his spirit \ft or \fq his soul\f*
\s1 Reason's Sovereignty in the Seven
Since, then, the seven brothers despised sufferings even unto death, everyone must concede that devout reason is sovereign over the emotions.
For if they had been slaves to their emotions and had eaten defiling food, we would say that they had been conquered by these emotions.
But in fact it was not so. Instead, by reason, which is praised before God, they prevailed over their emotions.
The supremacy of the mind over these cannot be overlooked, for the brothers\f + \fr 13.4  \ft Gk \fq they \f* mastered both emotions and pains.
How then can one fail to confess the sovereignty of right reason over emotion in those who were not turned back by fiery agonies?
For just as towers jutting out over harbors hold back the threatening waves and make it calm for those who sail into the inner basin,
so the seven-towered right reason of the youths, by fortifying the harbor of religion, conquered the tempest of the emotions.
For they constituted a holy chorus of religion and encouraged one another, saying,
“Brothers, let us die like brothers for the sake of the law; let us imitate the three youths in Assyria who despised the same ordeal of the furnace.
Let us not be cowardly in the demonstration of our piety.”
While one said, “Courage, brother,” another said, “Bear up nobly,”
and another reminded them, “Remember whence you came, and the father by whose hand Isaac would have submitted to being slain for the sake of religion.”

Each of them and all of them together looking at one another, cheerful and undaunted, said, “Let us with all our hearts consecrate ourselves to God, who gave us our lives,\f + \fr 13.13  \ft Or \fq souls \f* and let us use our bodies as a bulwark for the law.
for great is the struggle of the soul and the danger of eternal torment lying before those who transgress the commandment of God.
Therefore let us put on the full armor of self-control, which is divine reason.
For if we so die,\f + \fr 13.17  \ft Other ancient authorities read \fq suffer \f* Abraham and Isaac and Jacob will welcome us, and all the fathers will praise us.”
Those who were left behind said to each of the brothers who were being dragged away, “Do not put us to shame, brother, or betray the brothers who have died before us.”
You are not ignorant of the affection of family ties, which the divine and all-wise Providence has bequeathed through the fathers to their descendants and which was implanted in the mother's womb.

There each of the brothers spent the same length of time and was shaped during the same period of time; and growing from the same blood and through the same life, they were brought to the light of day.
When they were born after an equal time of gestation, they drank milk from the same fountains. From such embraces brotherly-loving souls are nourished;
and they grow stronger from this common nurture and daily companionship, and from both general education and our discipline in the law of God.
Therefore, when sympathy and brotherly affection had been so established, the brothers were the more sympathetic to one another.
Since they had been educated by the same law and trained in the same virtues and brought up in right living, they loved one another all the more.
A common zeal for nobility strengthened their goodwill toward one another, and their concord,
because they could make their brotherly love more fervent with the aid of their religion.

But although nature and companionship and virtuous habits had augmented the affection of family ties, those who were left endured for the sake of religion, while watching their brothers being maltreated and tortured to death.
Furthermore, they encouraged them to face the torture, so that they not only despised their agonies, but also mastered the emotions of brotherly love.
O reason,\f + \fr 14.2  \ft Or \fq O minds\f* more royal than kings and freer than the free!
O sacred and harmonious concord of the seven brothers on behalf of religion!
None of the seven youths proved coward or shrank from death,
but all of them, as though running the course toward immortality, hastened to death by torture.
Just as the hands and feet are moved in harmony with the guidance of the mind, so those holy youths, as though moved by an immortal spirit of devotion, agreed to go to death for its sake.
O most holy seven, brothers in harmony! For just as the seven days of creation move in choral dance around religion,
so these youths, forming a chorus, encircled the sevenfold fear of tortures and dissolved it.

Even now, we ourselves shudder as we hear of the suffering of these young men; they not only saw what was happening, not only heard the direct word of threat, but also bore the sufferings patiently, and in agonies of fire at that.

What could be more excruciatingly painful than this? For the power of fire is intense and swift, and it consumed their bodies quickly.   
\s1 An Encomium on the Mother of the Seven
Do not consider it amazing that reason had full command over these men in their tortures, since the mind of woman despised even more diverse agonies,
for the mother of the seven young men bore up under the rackings of each one of her children.
Observe how complex is a mother's love for her children, which draws everything toward an emotion felt in her inmost parts.
Even unreasoning animals, as well as human beings, have a sympathy and parental love for their offspring.
For example, among birds, the ones that are tame protect their young by building on the housetops,
and the others, by building in precipitous chasms and in holes and tops of trees, hatch the nestlings and ward off the intruder.
